content: A coronary risk profile is a series of blood tests designed to measure cholesterol and triglyceride levels. These tests are used to assess an individual's risk for developing heart disease. To perform a coronary risk profile, blood is typically drawn from a vein, most commonly from the inside of the elbow or the back of the hand. The area is first cleaned with an antiseptic solution to prevent infection. A healthcare provider then applies an elastic band around the upper arm to increase pressure and make the vein more prominent. A needle is gently inserted into the vein, and blood is collected into an airtight vial or tube. Once the blood is collected, the elastic band is removed, the needle is withdrawn, and the puncture site is covered to stop any bleeding. In infants or young children, a lancet may be used to puncture the skin and collect blood. The blood is then gathered into a small glass tube (pipette), onto a slide, or on a test strip. A bandage may be applied if there is any bleeding. The collected blood is sent to a laboratory for analysis. The following components are measured: Low-density lipoprotein (LDL), often referred to as bad cholesterol. High-density lipoprotein (HDL), known as good cholesterol. Total cholesterol. Triglycerides. Very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), which is often calculated based on triglyceride levels. Some laboratories may also include additional tests, such as C-reactive protein (CRP), to provide further insights. To prepare for a coronary risk profile, you should avoid eating or drinking anything except water for 9 to 12 hours before the blood draw. When the needle is inserted to draw blood, some individuals may experience moderate pain, while others may feel only a slight prick or stinging sensation. After the procedure, there may be some throbbing at the puncture site. A coronary risk profile is performed for several reasons: To screen adults and children for high cholesterol and triglyceride levels. To monitor individuals with previously diagnosed high cholesterol who are undergoing treatment. For adults, the first screening is typically done between the ages of 20 and 35 for men and 20 and 45 for women, though recommendations may vary by medical organization. Follow-up screenings are generally recommended every five years. Screening is also performed for individuals who develop conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, or other illnesses related to atherosclerosis. Follow-up testing is used to evaluate the effectiveness of dietary changes and medications in managing high cholesterol. For children, screening recommendations are less consistent. Some experts suggest screening only those with risk factors, such as a family history of high cholesterol or early heart disease (e.g., heart attacks before age 55 in men or before age 65 in women). The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force states that there is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against cholesterol screening in children. Normal results for a coronary risk profile vary depending on whether the individual has coronary artery disease or other risk factors. For adults, the desired values are: LDL: 70–130 mg/dL (lower values are better). HDL: Greater than 40–60 mg/dL (higher values are better). Total cholesterol: Less than 200 mg/dL (lower values are better). Triglycerides: 10–150 mg/dL (lower values are better). VLDL: 2–38 mg/dL. For children, consult your healthcare provider for ideal levels. Note that normal value ranges may vary slightly between laboratories, so it is important to discuss your specific results with your doctor. Abnormal results may indicate an increased risk for atherosclerosis and related conditions, including: Heart disease. Kidney disease. Poor blood supply to the legs. Stroke. The risks associated with a coronary risk profile are minimal. However, veins and arteries vary in size between individuals and even between different sides of the body, which can make obtaining a blood sample more challenging in some cases.
